edges.description: Reduced TCF4 E-protein dosage impairs proneural bHLH heterodimer transcriptional output during neurogenesis and glial differentiation.
Loss of TCF4 transcriptional repression derepresses ectopic SCN10A (Nav1.8) expression in central neurons.
TCF4 deficiency downregulates presynaptic RIMBP2 expression and impairs cortical synaptic transmission.
TCF4 haploinsufficiency disrupts development and CO2/H+ chemosensitivity of Phox2b+ parafacial and retrotrapezoid brainstem respiratory neurons.
TCF4 haploinsufficiency impairs enteric autonomic nervous system function and intestinal motility.
TCF4 haploinsufficiency is associated with a wide mouth as part of the PTHS facial gestalt, although the intermediate craniofacial developmental mechanism is unknown.
TCF4 haploinsufficiency is associated with fleshy, everted lips with a thick vermilion border, although the intermediate craniofacial mechanism is unknown.
TCF4 haploinsufficiency is associated with deeply set eyes, although the intermediate craniofacial developmental mechanism is unknown.
TCF4 haploinsufficiency is associated with a prominent/beaked nasal bridge, although the intermediate craniofacial developmental mechanism is unknown.
TCF4 haploinsufficiency is associated with anteverted nares, although the intermediate craniofacial developmental mechanism is unknown.
TCF4 haploinsufficiency is associated with a single transverse palmar crease, although the intermediate limb/dermatoglyphic developmental mechanism is unknown.
TCF4 haploinsufficiency causes early-onset severe myopia, although the intermediate ocular refractive developmental mechanism is unknown.
TCF4 haploinsufficiency is associated with frequent astigmatism, although the intermediate corneal/refractive developmental mechanism is unknown.
TCF4 haploinsufficiency is associated with frequent strabismus, although the intermediate oculomotor mechanism is unknown.
Impaired cortical neurogenesis and circuit assembly cause moderate-to-severe intellectual disability.
Defective neuronal and glial differentiation delays motor and cognitive milestone acquisition from infancy.
Disrupted cortical and speech-motor circuit development results in absent or severely restricted expressive speech.
Reduced postnatal cortical neurogenesis, gliogenesis, and neuropil expansion lead to secondary microcephaly.
Impaired cortical neuronal differentiation and interhemispheric axon tract development result in hypoplasia or aplasia of the corpus callosum.
Impaired central motor-pathway maturation manifests as infantile and childhood hypotonia.
Neuromuscular hypotonia and altered motor-pathway maturation predispose to scoliosis, although the specific axial mechanism in PTHS is unknown.
Disrupted cerebellar and motor-network differentiation causes gait and truncal motor incoordination/ataxia.
Altered corticostriatal neurodevelopment produces repetitive stereotypic hand and motor movements.
Perturbed cortical differentiation and circuit development underlie autism spectrum behavioral manifestations.
Loss of expiratory parafacial neurons and impaired retrotrapezoid CO2/H+ chemosensitivity cause awake bouts of hyperventilation.
Disrupted brainstem respiratory rhythm generation and chemosensitivity cause recurrent awake breath-holding and apneic episodes.
Impaired enteric autonomic intestinal motility causes chronic, often severe constipation.
Upper gastrointestinal autonomic dysmotility predisposes to frequent gastroesophageal reflux.
Oromotor and upper gastrointestinal dysmotility drive persistent feeding difficulties from infancy.
Persistent feeding difficulties, reflux, and gastrointestinal dysmotility impair caloric intake and postnatal weight gain, leading to failure to thrive.
Aberrant central Nav1.8 channel expression perturbs brainstem respiratory neuron excitability, contributing to disordered breathing.
Altered intrinsic neuronal sodium-channel excitability contributes to network hyperexcitability and seizure susceptibility.
Impaired cortical synaptic transmission and homeostatic plasticity degrade cognitive network processing.
Defective cortical network excitability and homeostatic synaptic plasticity predispose to epilepsy.
Disrupted cortical and autonomic synaptic network regulation contributes to sleep initiation and maintenance disturbances.

nodes.description: In patient-derived cortical neurons, TCF4 mutations impair spontaneous synaptic transmission, network excitability, and homeostatic plasticity. The presynaptic binding protein RIMBP2 is the most differentially expressed gene, and restoring presynaptic RIMBP2 rescues the synaptic deficits, implicating dysregulated presynaptic function as an early pathophysiology.

evidence.reference_title: TCF4 Mutations Disrupt Synaptic Function Through Dysregulation of RIMBP2 in Patient-Derived Cortical Neurons.
evidence.snippet: Cortical neurons derived from patients with TCF4 mutations showed deficits in spontaneous synaptic transmission, network excitability, and homeostatic plasticity.

evidence.reference_title: TCF4 Mutations Disrupt Synaptic Function Through Dysregulation of RIMBP2 in Patient-Derived Cortical Neurons.
evidence.snippet: identified the presynaptic binding protein RIMBP2 as the most differentially expressed gene in PTHS neurons. Remarkably, TCF4-dependent deficits in spontaneous synaptic transmission and network excitability were rescued by increasing RIMBP2 expression in presynaptic neurons.

nodes.description: SCN10A, encoding the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.8, is a downstream target of TCF4 that is consistently upregulated in central neurons in PTHS mouse models. Ectopic Nav1.8 sodium conductance alters intrinsic neuronal excitability and brainstem/cortical circuit function, and pharmacological Nav1.8 inhibition normalizes neuron function, respiratory stability, and behavioral abnormalities in models.

evidence.reference_title: Evaluation of Nav1.8 as a therapeutic target for Pitt Hopkins Syndrome
evidence.snippet: Here, we propose that SCN10A is an important target gene of TCF4 that is an applicable therapeutic approach for PTHS. Scn10a encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.8 and is consistently shown to be upregulated in PTHS mouse models.
